title: 0-1 Knapsack and choice-based DP
overview: 0-1 knapsack is the classic 'take it or leave it' DP: for each item you either put it in the bag or skip it, and you keep the better result. The state is (item index, remaining capacity), which you memoize in a 2D table. The practice day uses the same 'make a choice, keep the best' idea on grid paths, stairs, house robbing and Pascal's triangle.

concepts.explain: `knapsack(i, w)` = the best value using items 0..i with capacity w left. The answer is `knapsack(n-1, W)`.
If item i fits, compare taking it (`val[i] + knapsack(i-1, w - weight[i])`) with skipping it (`knapsack(i-1, w)`). If it does not fit, you can only skip.
No items left (`i < 0`) or no capacity left: value 0.
There are n x (W+1) states. Fill `dp` with -1 for **every** capacity 0..W, including W itself, then store each result the first time.
concepts.snippet: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j <= W; j++) dp[i][j] = -1;

concepts.explain: Max path sum (go down or right), min cost stairs (come from one or two steps back), house robber (rob this house + best two back, or skip) all follow 'best of the choices'.
When a state only needs the previous one or two states, two variables replace the whole table.

files.title: 0-1 knapsack with plain recursion
files.what: The recursive take-or-skip solution without memoization. It computes the best value but never prints it.
steps: Read `n`, the `val` array, the `weight` array, then `max_weight`.
If `weight[i] <= w`, return the max of taking and skipping item `i`.
Otherwise return the skip option only.
files.input_note: n, the n values, the n weights, then the capacity.
files.output_note: Nothing is printed: the result of `knapsack(n-1, max_weight)` is thrown away. The correct answer for this input is 90 (items of weight 3 and 5).
files.watch_out: Wrap the call in `cout << ... << endl;` to see the answer.

check.a: Each item branches into two calls, so n items give up to 2^n calls, and the same (i, w) pairs are recomputed.

files.title: 0-1 knapsack with memoization
files.what: Adds a `dp[i][w]` table to the recursion so each state is solved once, and prints the result.
steps: Fill `dp[i][j] = -1` to mark states as unsolved.
In `knapsack`, return `dp[i][w]` if it is already known.
Otherwise compute take/skip, store the result in `dp[i][w]`, and return it.
files.input_note: n, values, weights, capacity. The right answer is 90.
files.output_note: Prints `0`, which is wrong: see Watch out.
files.watch_out: The init loop is `j < max_weight`, so `dp[i][max_weight]` keeps its global value 0 instead of -1. The very first call `knapsack(n-1, max_weight)` sees 0, thinks it is already solved, and returns 0. Fix: `j <= max_weight`.

check.q: How many different states can this function visit?
check.a: About n x (W+1): every item index combined with every capacity from 0 to W.

files.title: Knapsack in the judge's input format
files.what: Same memoized knapsack, but reads `N W` first and then one `weight value` pair per line, like the judge.
steps: Same init loop and memoized recursion as `knapsack_using_dp.cpp`.
files.output_note: Prints `0` instead of 90, because of the same init bug.
files.watch_out: `j < max_weight` should be `j <= max_weight`; otherwise `dp[n-1][W]` looks solved with value 0.

check.q: Which single character fixes this program?
check.a: Changing `<` to `<=` in the dp init loop.

files.title: Practice: Knapsack (judge version)
files.what: The same solution again with arrays sized to the judge's limits (N <= 20, W <= 100).
steps: Same init loop and take/skip recursion.
files.output_note: Prints `0` instead of 90 for the same reason as the other versions.
files.watch_out: Init with `j <= max_weight`. After the fix it prints 90.

check.a: N is at most 20 and W at most 100, so a little extra room covers every (i, w) pair.

files.title: The maximum path-sum (grid DP)

problem.name: Codeforces Group - X. The maximum path-sum

files.what: From the top-left cell you may only move down or right. `maxPathSum(i, j)` = this cell + the better of going down or right, memoized in `dp`.
steps: Reaching the bottom-right cell returns its value (base case).
On the last row you can only go right; on the last column only down.
Otherwise take `matrix[i][j] + max(down, right)` and store it.
files.input_note: N M, then the grid. This is the judge's example (expected 24).
files.watch_out: Values can be negative, so -1 is not a perfectly safe 'unsolved' marker: a real answer of -1 would be recomputed (still correct, only slower). A separate `bool done[][]` avoids that.

check.q: Why can't you just go greedily to the bigger neighbour each step?
check.a: A small step now can lead to large values later. Here 5 -> 2 looks better than 5 -> 1, but the 1 leads to the 9.

files.title: LeetCode 746: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
files.what: Bottom-up with two variables: the cheapest way to stand on position i is the cheaper of coming from i-2 (paying `cost[i-2]`) or from i-1 (paying `cost[i-1]`).
steps: `first` and `second` are the best costs to reach positions i-2 and i-1; both start at 0 because you may start on step 0 or 1 for free.
After the loop, `second` is the cost to reach position n (the top).
files.input_note: The length, then the costs. This is LeetCode's Example 2 (expected 6).
files.watch_out: The file only holds the `Solution` class (no includes, no `main`); the page adds a test driver.

check.q: For `cost = [10, 15, 20]`, what is the answer and why?
check.a: 15: start on step 1, pay 15, and jump two steps to the top.

files.title: LeetCode 198: House Robber
files.what: `dp[i]` = the most money from houses 0..i. Either rob house i (then add `dp[i-2]`) or skip it (keep `dp[i-1]`). The file has its own `main` testing both LeetCode examples.
files.input_note: No input; the two examples are written inside `main`.
files.output_note: `Example 1 output: 4` and `Example 2 output: 12`, matching LeetCode's expected answers.

check.a: 4: rob the first and last houses (2 + 2).

files.title: LeetCode 118: Pascal's Triangle
files.what: Each row starts and ends with 1; every inner value is the sum of the two values above it in the previous row. The file's `main` prints 5 rows.
steps: `main` prints each row on its own line.
files.output_note: Five lines from `1` to `1 4 6 4 1`, matching LeetCode's first example.

recap: 0-1 knapsack: state (i, w), choices take or skip, keep the max.
Base case: no items or no capacity gives 0.
Memo table must be initialised for every capacity **0..W inclusive**.
Many DP problems are 'best of a few choices' from smaller states.
If a state needs only the last one or two states, two variables are enough.

check_yourself.a: 9: take the items of weight 3 and 4 (4 + 5). Weight 5 + weight 1 gives only 8.
Each item is taken 0 times or 1 time; you cannot take a fraction or several copies.

check_yourself.q: What is the time complexity of memoized knapsack with n = 100 and W = 1000?
check_yourself.a: About n x W = 100,000 states, each O(1), so it is fast.

body: You are packing a bag that carries 5 kg. Three things lie on the table, each with a weight and a price, and you want the most valuable bag you can carry. Nothing can be cut in half: each item goes in whole or stays behind. That is why it is called **0-1** knapsack — for every item the answer is 0 or 1, leave it or take it.

Done by hand you would try every combination: eight of them for three items. Items 0 and 1 weigh 5 kg together and are worth 7, and nothing beats that, so 7 is the answer. But every extra item doubles the number of combinations, so forty items is about a million million of them — 2^n again, the same wall as plain Fibonacci in the last module.

So stop thinking about combinations and think about one item at a time. Stand in front of item `i` with `w` kg of space left. There are at most two moves. Leave it, and your value is whatever the earlier items can give with the same `w` kg. Take it, if it fits, and your value is its own price plus whatever the earlier items can give with `w - weight[i]` kg. Keep the larger.
The question "best value using items 0 to `i` with `w` kg left?" is the **state**, and those two moves are the arrows out of it.

States repeat here exactly as `fib(3)` repeated, so you memoise them. The only difference is that this question needs two numbers to describe it, `i` and `w`, so the notebook is a 2D table: one row per "items allowed up to here", one column per "space still in the bag".

Fill it row by row, reading each cell as a contest between the two moves and always looking one row up. Row `items 0..1`, column 5: leaving item 1 gives the 3 one row up in column 5; taking it gives its price 4 plus the 3 one row up in column `5 - 3 = 2`, so 7, and taking wins. In the last row, column 4: leaving gives 4, taking gives 5 plus column 0, so taking wins with 5. But in column 5 of that row, leaving gives 7 and taking only 5, so the 7 stays.

**Why the bottom-right cell is the answer.** Read its two labels. The bottom row means every item was offered; the rightmost column means the bag was empty when you started. "Best value when all three items were on the table and you had the full 5 kg" is word for word the question you were asked, so the 7 sitting there is it — the same pair you found by hand, reached in 18 cells rather than 8 guesses. The gap widens fast: 40 items and a 100 kg bag is about 4000 cells against a million million combinations.

**What is new since Module 14.** There the state was a single number and fed the next one in a fixed way. Here every state makes a real choice and you keep the better branch. That pattern is the rest of the day in different clothes: a grid path where at each cell you go down or right and keep the bigger sum, a staircase reached from one step back or two, houses where you rob this one plus the best two back or skip it.

Two practical points. The memo table must be set to -1 for every capacity from 0 to `W`, `W` included; a loop that stops one column short leaves a stale cell behind and the answer goes wrong without any warning. And when a state depends only on the previous one or two states, you do not need the table at all — two variables will do.
The programs below build knapsack twice, plain then memoised, then put the same take-or-leave thinking to work on five more problems.
